summary:
FireLedger is an interactive wildfire observation explorer that helps people investigate when and where satellite fire detections occur. Users can import Canadian NASA FIRMS data by choosing a date range and satellites, or load FIRMS ZIP archives and prepared observation files. The map groups nearby detections so broad patterns are easy to scan, then reveals individual observation footprints and details as users zoom in.

A timeline, playback controls, date filters, and observation calendar help users follow activity over time. The 2D map shows geographic patterns, while the 3D space–time view makes timing differences and possible movement easier to explore. FireLedger also highlights thermal overlap and repeat detections, and draws scored candidate links between observations to help identify detections that may be related. These links are investigative clues, not confirmed fire tracks or probability estimates.

The Measure tool calculates the area of a drawn region or the distance along a path, helping users focus on places and compare spatial patterns. Processing data in the browser gives users direct control over imported files and supports private, hands-on exploration. 
Aside from the project, we would like to give everyone at Space Apps a massive thank you for this opportunity. Just the fact that you guys set up the environment was amazing. You already had us hooked the moment you mentioned pizza XD. Thank you from our team!
details:
During this project, our team, "The A-Team" decided to tackle the challenge of Harmonizing the incompatibility of the data of the

older sensor, MODIS, that will be soon decommissioned and be fully replaced by the newer one named VIIRS.

To achieve that result we:

- Parsed data from both Fire Detection instruments (VIIRS and MODIS satellites)

- Created a master table that mapped each Measurement taken by one satellite with another as long as their “datetime_utc” matched

- From the Master Table, we generated a new Unified lossy format were both dataset are now relative to each other in term of fields and values

- Using this Unified format, we have drawn a 3d temporal map (x: latitude, y longitude, z time) and overlaid it on the Canadian map (timespan: 1st-7th June 2023, Canadian Wildfire) to observe the start and end of extreme fire activity mostly depicting fire

- Using the 3d temporal map creating a linkage between the distinct fire and their evolution through time, we were able to create Interpolation measurements that predict where/and how fast a current fire will spread at an instant_t. Useful during down time between two distinct satellite readings.

Our solution addresses the challenge by harmonizing both dataset in a unified but lossy format.  Predict using an interpolation strategy to approximate how a fire could/will grow. Using that information and passing it to first respondent and firefighter, this could allow faster response time that could save life.


FireLedger is a browser based tool for exploring NASA satellite fire detections across Canada. Users can import NASA FIRMS data by selecting satellites and a UTC date range, upload FIRMS archive ZIP files, or open prepared observation files. The data is processed in the browser and shown on an interactive map.

The 2D map places detections at their recorded locations and displays approximate sensor footprints. Nearby observations group together when zoomed out, helping users spot broad patterns before inspecting individual detections. A timeline, playback controls, calendar, and date filters help users follow observations across time. The 3D view places time on a vertical axis, so users can explore the gaps and patterns between satellite passes. Height represents time, not terrain elevation.

FireLedger also displays thermal overlap and repeat detections, and calculates ranked candidate links between observations using factors such as distance, elapsed time, sensor footprint, confidence, and detection type. These links help users investigate possible relationships. They are not confirmed fire tracks or probabilities. The Measure tool calculates the area of a drawn region or the distance along a path, helping users focus exploration on a location.

The project is designed to make satellite observations easier to inspect while keeping their uncertainty visible. Detection footprints are approximate, satellite observations can have gaps, and thermal signals do not establish a fire perimeter. The intended impact is to help students, researchers, and interested communities explore where and when detections occurred and identify patterns for further investigation.

FireLedger is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses browser based graphics and background processing to handle mapping and data analysis on the user’s device. The team considered varied sensor footprints, different observation times, large datasets, and the risk of presenting possible links as confirmed events.

To achieve our objective and solve the challenge, we decided to parse the .csv data of both Fire detection instruments using python. Then, by doing some data cleaning, we decided to drop fields that couldn’t cleanly be aligned with their counterpart/relative equivalent on the other Satellite sensor or simply to keep the scope of the project reasonable for our current personal ability. Talking about scope, we limited ourselves to work with data from a specific timeframe: 7 days from the june 1st to the june 7th of 2023 in Canada during the Wildfire that was experienced there at the time.

In more details, we first inspected the .csv format in which the data of each sensor were written to understand their context. 

https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/content/descriptions/FIRMS_VIIRS_Firehotspots.html

VIIRS format: Latitude, Longitude, Bright_ti4 / Brightness, Scan, Track, Acq_Date, Acq_Time, Satellite, Confidence, Version, Bright_ti5 / Brightness_2, FRP, Type, DayNight

https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/content/descriptions/FIRMS_MODIS_Firehotspots.html

MODIS format: longitude, latitude, datetime_utc, radius_km, brightness_k, confidence_raw, type, source_id

Then using python, we parsed those data and created a master table that mapped each measurement reading to clearly highlight the provenance of each set and prepare the ground up to unify them in the next phase.

Master table design:

| source_id | Satellite | Instrument |

|---|---|---|

| 0 | Terra | MODIS |

| 1 | Aqua | MODIS |

| 2 | Suomi NPP (S-NPP) | VIIRS |

| 3 | NOAA-20 (JPSS-1) | VIIRS |

| 4 | NOAA-21 (JPSS-2) | VIIRS |

Master table filled with data:

source_id,satellite,instrument

0,Terra,MODIS

1,Aqua,MODIS

2,Suomi-NPP,VIIRS

3,NOAA-20,VIIRS

4,NOAA-21,VIIRS

We then remapped both sensor data in a unified new lossy format (lossy because we scrapped some field for scope and simplicity and because many mapped fields aren’t a one-for-one due to difference of precision between their hardware).

New Unified lossy format: longitude, latitude, datetime_utc, radius_km, brightness_k, confidence_raw, type, source_id

Spatial Coordinate rounding used to build that lossy format: 5°x5°x 1 month

Transformation applied on the data during construction of this lossy format: We modify everything reading into points. We are not using an uniform pixel size, but consider it as a circle. So our first version is going to be a 2d map, with circles. We circle when the fire has been measured. We show the user like layers of detected data, then we do a "best fit". Use 3D geometry to build like a cylinder by connecting the disks, and we decide if we keep it as a fire movement or we don't trust it and consider it as two different fires. According to time like in chronological order, we have the position of each satellite and the data. However, we just mark it as a disk with a set radius, and one id for what the satellite is, so for the format we would have x coor, y coor, time, radius, brightness (with an algorithm that transforms the brightness of each instrument into temperature), source id.

Formula to transform pixel (square) to circle: pi r^2 = scan x track, so r = root(scan x track/pi)

The circle has the same area as the satellite pixel: ar

shows the observation footprint not the fire's measured size.

scan x track/r. 

Using those foundations we created a temporal map (3 axis: x for latitude, y for longitude and z for time) that we overlaid upon the geographical zone of Canada during the 2023 wildfire of june where we can see the fire appeared and spread before dying. From Looking at these “linkages” of disk (disk represent the coverage of the fire on a surface of the map) , we can see that they form a 2 cones flipped on top of one another (peak of cone: start or end of fire depending on the position on the time axis, were earlier means start) (base of the cone: maximum coverage size that the fire had).

Following that, from those 3d temporal maps, we implemented an interpolation mechanism that allows us to predict the growth rate and the progressing/decreasing evolution of the coverage of a fire at a specific location. This applied even when the satellite imaging were not available due to their intermittent nature because they rotate across the Earth and read the same locations at hours of interval.

Lastly, we create a web interface that allow first responder and scientist to read and interpret the data easily. This could allow them to extrapolate the growth of similar fire in the future and hopefully allow then to react appropriately to help the population and control the fire as soon as possible.
